title: Are you doing Romanian deadlifts wrong?
summary: NH contrasts the popular RDL (minimal knee bend, hip hinge, stops below the knee) with the version he learned in Europe: a full-range 'reverse deadlift' starting from the rack with a slow negative to just above the floor. He explains what each offers, recommends his version for higher reps on a separate day to train the deadlift negative, and argues the popular RDL is really a stiff-legged deadlift negative.

claims.claim: The most-viewed YouTube RDL tutorials show minimal knee bend, lots of hip travel backward, a stretch on lower back and hamstrings, ending just below the kneecap.
In his country/Europe the RDL was taught as a reverse deadlift: negative first from the rack, full range until the plates almost touch the ground, then back up; this is how NH does them.
The popular short-range RDL allows heavy loads, sometimes more than a conventional deadlift, by using the stretch reflex and a short range, especially for short-femured lifters.
The full-range reverse deadlift forces much lighter loads because, as reps accumulate, the positive portions become increasingly taxing.
The popular RDL is a 'pure hinge' with almost no knee or quad involvement, giving a better stretch, usually done for very low reps.
On regular deadlifts you should not fight the negative; let gravity bring the bar down, since a deadlift rep is floor to lockout and resisting the descent taxes your positives.
Skipping deadlift negatives leaves a portion of the movement untrained; doing slow-negative deadlifts from the rack on another day fills that gap.
Rack-start slow-negative deadlifts also aid recovery since you don't pull from the floor, while still giving a deadlift-like stimulus at higher reps.
Do the full-range reverse-deadlift style of RDL with higher reps.

Most people doing RDLs are really doing stiff-legged deadlifts; the RDL is essentially the negative portion of a stiff-leg deadlift, so the separate name is semantically odd, though too entrenched to change.
